overview.title: 📖 Overview: Locating the Real Dispute, Then Blemished Offerings
overview.subtitle: Temurah 6a–6b
overview.hebrewSource: כִּי קָא מִיפַּלְגִי אַבָּיֵי וְרָבָא בְּשִׁינּוּי קוֹנֶה
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf completes the long run of test cases for Abaye and Rava's dispute — robbery of altered goods, seized collateral, and pe'ah given from dough — each reconciled with its own verse. Rav Aḥa then asks the pointed question: if every case has been explained away, what do Abaye and Rava actually disagree about in practice? The Gemara settles on fixed interest, though even that is reframed as a dispute over verses (Rabbi Elazar vs. Rabbi Yoḥanan) rather than the theory itself, concluding that Abaye and Rava differ only in their default assumption when no verse says otherwise. The daf then pivots to a new topic: the five (or six) separate prohibitions violated by consecrating a blemished animal for the altar, and a detailed study of the Yom Kippur scapegoat's own blemish-exemption.

slides.title: 🪵 More Test Cases for the General Rule
slides.subtitle: Robbery, collateral, and pe'ah each get their own reconciling verse
rows: Robbery: stolen wood made into vessels
Robber keeps the vessels, pays value at time of theft
"That which he took by robbery" (Lev. 5:23) — return required only if unchanged
Collateral seized in violation of the law
Creditor must return items the debtor needs, by day or night
"הָשֵׁב תָּשִׁיב" (doubled verb) — return required, but not permanently
Pe'ah not separated until dough is kneaded
Poor still receive pe'ah even from the dough
"תַּעֲזוֹב" written twice (Lev. 19:10, 23:22) — obligation persists at every stage

callout.label: Running theme:
callout.text: Each apparent exception is folded back into the rule its proponent favors — Abaye's 'effective by default' or Rava's 'ineffective by default.'

slides.title: 💰 So What DO They Disagree About?
slides.subtitle: Rav Aḥa's challenge to Rav Ashi

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rav Aḥa, son of Rava, asks Rav Ashi: now that every case has been explained away with its own verse, where do Abaye and Rava actually differ in practice?
2️⃣ First answer: fixed interest (ribbit ketzutza) — must a court forcibly return it to the borrower?

3️⃣ But this too turns out to map onto an earlier dispute of Rabbi Elazar (returned) and Rabbi Yoḥanan (not returned), each with independent verses — not a pure consequence of 'effective vs. ineffective'
4️⃣ Final answer: Abaye and Rava disagree only theoretically, in שִׁינּוּי קוֹנֶה — the default assumption when the Torah gives no specific verse either way

callout.label: Bottom line:
callout.text: Abaye's default: a forbidden act, absent a stated exception, is presumed effective. Rava's default: it is presumed ineffective.

slides.title: 📈 Fixed Interest: Two Amoraic Layers
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yoḥanan's dispute maps loosely onto Rava and Abaye

boxes.title: Rabbi Elazar (≈ Rava)
items: Fixed interest paid IS repossessed by the court
Source: 'that your brother may live with you' — the interest must return so the debtor can live alongside the lender
The forbidden act did not effectively transfer ownership

boxes.title: Rabbi Yoḥanan (≈ Abaye)
items: Even fixed interest is NOT repossessed by the court
Source: Ezekiel 18:13 — the usurer 'shall not live' (punished with death), but the money is not said to be returned
Also compared to a bloodshedder — an irreversible wrong

callout.label: Complication:
callout.text: Abaye himself holds fixed interest IS forcibly returned in a mixed cloak/interest case — showing this dispute is driven by its own verses, not simply by the general theory.

slides.title: 🐐 Does 'Unto the Lord' Include or Exclude the Scapegoat?
slides.subtitle: Two verses about burning a blemished animal, read in opposite directions

lines.speaker: Baraita
lines.text: 'Nor make an offering by fire of them... unto the Lord' (Lev. 22:22) — 'unto the Lord' includes the scapegoat: even it may not be blemished, though it is never burned on the altar.

lines.speaker: Objection
lines.text: But elsewhere, in the law of slaughtering outside the Temple, 'unto the Lord' excludes — animals not exclusively dedicated to God (like the scapegoat) are excluded from that prohibition!

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: No contradiction: context decides the direction. There, the surrounding phrase already included broadly, so 'unto the Lord' narrows it. Here, the surrounding phrase ('fire') already excludes the scapegoat, so 'unto the Lord' broadens it back in.

lines.speaker: Further question
lines.text: But if the scapegoat is chosen only by a lottery between two fit goats, how could it ever have been blemished to begin with?

lines.speaker: Rava's answer
lines.text: The verse addresses a specific case: the scapegoat became blemished mid-day, after selection, and the priest transferred its sanctity to a replacement — that replacement still may not be blemished.

callout.label: Point:
callout.text: Even the scapegoat, chosen by lottery for a different fate than sacrifice, must still be physically unblemished.

slides.title: 🚫 Consecrating a Blemished Animal: Five Violations
slides.subtitle: Leviticus 22:20 is read to prohibit even the act of consecration itself
rows: בַּל תַּקְדִּישׁוּ
Consecrating a blemished animal for the altar at all
בַּל תַּקְרִיבוּ
Bringing it as an offering
בַּל תִּשְׁחֲטוּ
Slaughtering it as an offering
בַּל תִּזְרְקוּ
Sprinkling its blood on the altar
בַּל תַּקְטִירוּ (כּוּלּוֹ / מִקְצָתוֹ)
Burning all — or even part — of it on the altar
(R' Yosei b'R' Yehuda adds:) קַבָּלַת הַדָּם
Collecting its blood in a vessel

callout.label: Source:
callout.text: Each violation is drawn from a distinct phrase in Leviticus 22:20–22, showing that one act of misconduct can breach several separate biblical prohibitions.

summary.principle: After exhausting every test case, Abaye and Rava turn out to disagree only theoretically — the default assumption absent a specific verse — while consecrating a blemished animal for the altar violates five or six distinct prohibitions in its own right.

💰 Rav Aḥa: so what's the real dispute? → Fixed interest, though even that traces to Rabbi Elazar/Yoḥanan's own verses

columns.content: ⚖️ True dispute: the default when no verse specifies (shinuy koneh)
🚫 Blemished-animal consecration: 5-6 separate violations from one verse

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Abaye presumes forbidden acts work; Rava presumes they don't — only specific verses override each default

quiz.q: What verse does Rava use to explain why a robber who transforms stolen wood into vessels keeps the vessels but pays their value?
o: "You shall not rob"
"That which he took by robbery" (Lev. 5:23) — return is required only if the item is unchanged
"Hashev tashiv"
"Reishit"
quiz.e: Rava reads 'that which he took by robbery' as requiring restoration of the stolen item only if it remains as it was; once transformed, the robber acquires it by the change and just pays its value.

quiz.q: According to Rav Aḥa's question and the Gemara's eventual answer, what do Abaye and Rava actually disagree about in practice?
o: Nothing at all — they always agree
Only the theoretical default (shinuy koneh) applied when no specific verse addresses a case
Every single halakha in the Torah
Only laws of the Temple
quiz.e: After every apparent test case is reconciled by its own verse, the Gemara concludes that Abaye and Rava's dispute is purely about the default assumption when the Torah is silent — effective (Abaye) or ineffective (Rava).

quiz.q: What does Rabbi Yoḥanan's position on fixed interest (that it is not repossessed by the court) largely parallel?
o: Rava's view that forbidden acts are ineffective
Abaye's view that forbidden acts are effective
Neither Abaye nor Rava's view
Rabbi Elazar's view
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan holds fixed interest stays with the creditor once taken, paralleling Abaye's general presumption that a forbidden act still accomplishes something.

quiz.q: How many distinct Torah prohibitions does the baraita say are violated by consecrating a blemished animal for the altar (without Rabbi Yosei b'Rabbi Yehuda's addition)?
o: Two
Three
Five
Ten
quiz.e: The baraita lists five: not consecrating, not offering, not slaughtering, not sprinkling the blood, and not burning it (whole or in part) — Rabbi Yosei b'Rabbi Yehuda adds a sixth, collecting the blood.

quiz.q: According to Rava's resolution of the scapegoat exception, in what specific case does the verse 'unto the Lord' teach that a replacement scapegoat may not be blemished?
o: Whenever the original scapegoat is chosen by lottery
When the scapegoat becomes blemished after selection, mid-day, and the priest transfers its sanctity to a replacement
Never — the scapegoat can always be blemished
Only when the first goat has already been sacrificed
quiz.e: Rava explains the verse is needed for the case where the designated scapegoat becomes blemished during the day and its sanctity is transferred to a new goat — that replacement, too, must be unblemished.
